case.case_title: Bandara and Another v. Premachandra, Secretary, Ministry of Lands, Irrigation and Mahaweli Development and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 213/93, decided on 16 August 1993

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners were denied equal protection of the law under Article 12(1) by being treated differently and discriminatorily in their termination and denial of reinstatement compared to other public officers involved in similar trade union activities.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioners argued that their services were terminated and they were prevented from resuming their studies and work not for misconduct but for participating in trade union activity, and that this treatment was discriminatory and violated their fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the petitioners held office at pleasure under Article 55(1) and could be dismissed without assigning any reason, and that the Establishments Code provisions allowed termination without reason. They also argued the petitioners' misconduct justified dismissal and that the difference in treatment was rational due to the petitioners being trainees on probation and the public inconvenience caused by dismissing other officers.
key_facts: 22 petitioners selected for a four-year residential surveying degree course and appointed as Class III Grade III Surveyors on probation.
Petitioners participated in trade union work-to-rule campaign and submitted sick notes for absence.
Petitioners were served vacation of post notices and later informed their services were terminated without proper procedure or reason.
Other officers, including about 80 probationary surveyors and 1,000 permanent officers, participated in the same trade union action but faced no disciplinary action.
Petitioners were denied opportunity to submit explanations under the Establishments Code and were prevented from resuming studies and work.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 12(1) mandates fairness and excludes arbitrariness in dismissal and treatment of public officers. The 'pleasure principle' under Article 55(1) is subject to the equality provision of Article 12(1), meaning dismissal cannot be arbitrary or discriminatory. The Establishments Code provisions must be interpreted consistently with Article 12(1) and the rule of law, requiring a rational basis for differential treatment.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found that the petitioners were treated differently from other officers who engaged in similar trade union activities without facing dismissal or disciplinary action. The respondents failed to establish a rational basis for this difference. The petitioners were improperly deprived of procedural rights and dismissed not for misconduct but for trade union participation, violating their right to equal protection under the law.
principles_established: Dismissal of public officers under the 'pleasure principle' is subject to constitutional limitations including Article 12(1).
Rules made under Article 55(4) must be consistent with Article 12(1) and the rule of law.
Differential treatment of public officers requires a rational basis; arbitrary or discriminatory treatment violates Article 12(1).
Procedural fairness under the Establishments Code is part of the constitutional protection against arbitrary dismissal.
precedents_cited: A.G. v. Keyser's Royal Hotel [1920] AC 508

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were violated by discriminatory and arbitrary treatment in their dismissal and denial of reinstatement. The petitioners were entitled to reinstatement with seniority and arrears of salary, and compensation was awarded for the infringement.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Reinstatement of petitioners with effect from 7.12.92, payment of arrears of salary from 21.12.92, retention of seniority over subsequently admitted students, and Rs. 2,000/- compensation per petitioner for infringement of Article 12(1).

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the court's reasoning as it prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory treatment by the state, ensuring equal protection of the law. The petitioners' claim of discriminatory dismissal was directly assessed under this clause, leading to the court's decision to grant relief.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The court found that the petitioners were improperly and unlawfully prevented from resuming their studies and work, and that their dismissal was not for misconduct but for participation in trade union activity, violating their fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
